 As clean energy reshapes India's power landscape, a timeless technology is paving the way for a powerful new energy future. Often described as a water battery, pumped storage uses water and gravity to store electricity, bridging the gap between when power is generated and when it is needed. From reservoirs to modern grids, it is helping shape a cleaner, more reliable and resilient energy future. 

 
 

 
 

 


 Building India's Energy Future with Storage 


 India’s energy transition is increasingly anchored in renewable energy to strengthen energy security and sustainability. The country is rapidly expanding solar and wind capacity to meet rising electricity demand with cleaner sources. As of September 2026, India has 308.027 GW of installed non-fossil fuel-based electricity generation capacity. During FY 2025–26, India added around 55.29 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity. India has also set a target of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030. Solar and wind energy are going to make major contributions towards achieving this target . 


 However, renewable energy generation varies with sunlight, weather and daily demand patterns. This variability creates a growing need to store electricity when renewable generation exceeds demand. Energy storage can then supply electricity during periods of low renewable generation or peak demand. 


 As renewable capacity expands, the requirement for energy storage would also increase rapidly. The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) projects 73.93 GW of storage capacity by 2031–32. This includes 26.69 GW from Pumped Storage Projects (PSPs) and 47.24 GW from Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). 


 PSPs can play a crucial role in meeting this long-duration storage requirement. PSPs store electricity by pumping water to an upper reservoir during periods of surplus generation. The stored water is released through turbines when electricity demand rises. This enables PSPs to shift renewable electricity across time and support grid stability. They also provide long-duration storage and peaking support, making them important for integrating large renewable capacities. 


 


 
 
 
 
 Types of Energy Storage 


 Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and Pumped Storage Projects (PSPs) offer complementary solutions for integrating renewable energy into the grid. BESS can respond rapidly to short-duration requirements , supporting frequency regulation, peak management and grid balancing. PSPs provide long-duration storage , shifting large quantities of electricity across periods of surplus and demand. BESS can be deployed relatively quickly and close to renewable generation or consumption centres. PSPs require suitable geographical conditions but can provide large-scale storage over extended periods. Their long operating life also supports sustained grid infrastructure needs.

 A Pumped Storage Project typically consists of two reservoirs located at different elevations. When electricity is required, water is released from the upper reservoir through turbines to generate electricity. Once demand subsides, water is pumped back to the upper reservoir during periods of surplus electricity, completing the storage cycle. Pumped Storage Projects therefore function as large-scale energy storage systems and contribute to grid stability and renewable energy integration.

 Green hydrogen is emerging as a pillar of India’s clean energy transition. It is produced by splitting water using renewable electricity. It can help reduce emissions in sectors such as fertiliser production, petroleum refining, iron and steel manufacturing, heavy-duty road transport and shipping . The National Green Hydrogen Mission (NGHM) supports domestic manufacturing, production, assured demand and credible certification. From green ammonia auctions to India’s first hydrogen train, early projects point to a promising path. 

 
 

 
 

 


 Why Green Hydrogen 


 Hydrogen is an energy carrier that stores energy and delivers it for varied uses. In a fuel cell, it reacts with oxygen to produce electricity, leaving only water and heat as by-products, and no polluting compounds or greenhouse gases.Although pure hydrogen is not found in large quantities in nature, it can be extracted from compounds such as water or natural gas. Its environmental impact therefore depends on how it is made. Conventional methods rely on fossil fuels and release carbon emissions. 


 Production using renewable electricity from solar and wind power can cut this footprint substantially. Hydrogen made by splitting water using renewable power is called green hydrogen . Unlike fossil-based routes, this process emits far less carbon. India’s abundant solar and wind resources make domestic production feasible. This diversifies the country’s energy sources and strengthens energy security. 


 It also supports India’s goal of net-zero emissions by 2070.Green hydrogen matters most in sectors where cutting emissions is difficult. Reasons include high-temperature heat needs, chemical processes and few alternatives to fossil fuels. These hard-to-abate sectors include fertiliser, petroleum refining, iron and steel, heavy-duty road transport and shipping. Fertiliser and refining plants already use hydrogen, so green hydrogen can replace the fossil-based supply. It can also support lower-emission steelmaking, selected transport uses and energy storage. It is especially useful where direct electrification is difficult or less practical. 


 


 
 
 
 
 What Makes Hydrogen “Green” 


 Hydrogen releases no carbon dioxide when used, so its climate impact depends on how it is produced. In August 2023, the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) notified India’s Green Hydrogen Standard. Hydrogen qualifies as green if emissions do not exceed 2 kg of CO₂ equivalent per kg of hydrogen, on a well-to-gate basis, measured as a 12-month average. India thus became one of the first few countries to define green hydrogen formally. 


 

 
 

 
 

 For India, wider adoption could reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels. It would also lessen exposure to global fuel price swings. The sector could open opportunities in manufacturing, draw investment, create jobs and expand exports. Building capabilities across the value chain would strengthen domestic supply chains and spur industrial innovation. Green hydrogen can thus support self-reliance, sustainable industrial growth and a low-carbon future.

 Green hydrogen is produced mainly through water (H₂O) electrolysis. Electrolysis uses electricity to split a compound into simpler substances. Here, renewable electricity splits water into hydrogen (H₂) and oxygen (O₂), with minimal emissions.

A diaphragm keeps the gases apart while allowing ions to pass. When current flows , hydrogen forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. The gases are collected separately for further usage. An electrolyser thus turns renewable electricity and water into a low-emission fuel for industry, transport and other uses.

 The International Day for Biosphere Reserves celebrates the vital role these landscapes play in protecting biodiversity while sustaining human livelihoods. India’s 18 notified Biosphere Reserves, including 13 recognised by UNESCO, represent a wide variety of ecosystems, from the Western Ghats to high-altitude deserts and marine habitats. Their conservation efforts are supported by scientific research, community participation and government initiatives, demonstrating how environmental protection and human well-being can coexist. 




 


 Balancing Biodiversity Conservation with Sustainable Development 


 Biodiversity refers to the variability of living organisms across terrestrial, marine and other aquatic ecosystems. The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) recognises three levels of this diversity. Genetic diversity refers to variations within a species, such as different rice varieties. Species diversity reflects the range of species, such as tigers, elephants and orchids in a forest. Ecosystem diversity encompasses different natural habitats, including forests, grasslands, wetlands and coral reefs. Collectively, these levels sustain ecological processes and support life on Earth. 


 Biosphere reserves are areas identified by national governments for conserving biodiversity and promoting sustainable development. They protect natural habitats, maintain ecological balance and promote the sustainable use of biological resources. Their conservation contributes to food security, water availability, climate resilience and community livelihoods. They also safeguard natural resources for the benefit of future generations. 


 Recognising their global importance, the International Day for Biosphere Reserves is observed annually on 3 rd November . Proclaimed by UNESCO, the day highlights the contribution of these reserves to biodiversity conservation and sustainable development. It also promotes awareness of their role in reconciling environmental protection with human well-being. 


 For India, this observance reflects its commitment to protecting its rich natural heritage. As one of the world's 17 mega-biodiverse countries , India accounts for approximately 7–8% of recorded species worldwide , while it occupies only 2.4% of Earth's land area . Through its network of biosphere reserves, India seeks to strengthen ecological resilience and promote sustainable livelihoods. These efforts reflect the country's commitment to balancing conservation priorities with the developmental needs of local communities. 


 


 Biosphere Reserves: Understanding the Concept 


 Conserving biodiversity requires an approach that considers both natural ecosystems and the communities dependent on them. It also requires scientific research, responsible resource management and cooperation among different stakeholders. Biosphere reserves provide an internationally recognised framework for bringing these objectives together. 


 Launched in 1971, UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme promotes scientific approaches to improving relationships between people and their environment. Biosphere reserves function as living laboratories for testing and demonstrating sustainable development practices. They also help local communities sustain their livelihoods while living in harmony with nature. 


 


 
 How are Biosphere Reserves Different from Other Protected Areas? 


 Protected areas such as National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries primarily focus on protecting wildlife and their habitats under India’s wildlife protection laws. Biosphere reserves adopt a broader approach. They connect protected ecosystems with surrounding communities, making biosphere reserves a model for demonstrating how biodiversity and human well-being can coexist. 




 
 


 Functions of Biosphere Reserves 




 Biosphere reserves pursue 3 main functions: 


 
 Conservation: Protect biodiversity, genetic resources, ecosystems and landscapes, including associated cultural diversity. 

 Sustainable Economic Development: Encourage economic and social activities that respect ecological limits and local cultural values. 

 Scientific Support: Underpin scientific research, environmental monitoring, education, training and knowledge exchange to improve conservation practices. 

 

 


 
 The Three Interconnected Zones 




 Biosphere reserves follow a zonation model that balances different levels of protection and human activity. Each zone serves a distinct purpose, while contributing to the reserve’s overall objectives. 


 
 Core Area: The core area provides the highest level of protection for ecosystems and biodiversity. It conserves habitats, species and genetic diversity while maintaining essential ecological processes. Human activities are strictly limited, with compatible research and monitoring supporting long-term conservation. 

 Buffer Zone: The buffer zone surrounds or adjoins the core zone. It accommodates activities compatible with conservation, including environmental education, scientific research and regulated ecotourism. These activities improve ecological understanding while helping reduce pressures on strictly protected areas. 

 Transition Area: The transition area supports settlements, livelihoods and sustainable economic activities. Communities can practise responsible agriculture, sustainable forestry, ecotourism and other locally appropriate activities. This area promotes livelihoods while encouraging the sustainable use of natural resources.

 Khet Bachaao Abhiyaan (KBA)-Rabi 2026 is a nationwide campaign running from 22 October to 30 November 2026. Key priorities include balanced nutrient management, natural farming, crop residue management, crop diversification and climate-resilient agriculture. The campaign envisages 4,150 teams involving KVKs and ATMA, supported by over 12,000 scientists and ATMA functionaries. The initiative seeks to conduct 50,000 field demonstrations and 11,750 structured training sessions. The campaign projects a social media outreach of 1.5 crore farmers, with an envisaged expansion of overall digital outreach to 2.5 crore.

 Soil health is fundamental to agricultural productivity, food security, and rural livelihoods. With more than 46 percent of India’s workforce engaged in agriculture and allied activities, soil health influences food systems and economic stability. Healthy soils support higher crop yields and reduce dependence on external inputs. 


 Recognising the importance of soil health, Khet Bachaao Abhiyaan (KBA) - Rabi 2026 “Swasth Dhara, Samriddh Kisan” is envisaged as a nationwide campaign from 22 October to 30 November 2026. It follows a convergence-based approach, bringing together agricultural departments, research institutions, and field-level functionaries to promote balanced, judicious fertiliser use and sustainable nutrient management. The campaign aims to promote sustainable agriculture, improve soil health, and encourage the judicious use of agricultural resources. It also promotes natural farming, water conservation, and efficient use of natural resources. It addresses concerns such as imbalanced nutrient application, declining soil organic matter, rising cultivation costs, and the degradation of natural resources. 


 The initiatives also emphasise capacity building, farm mechanisation, and demonstrations of improved agricultural technologies, including regenerative agriculture practices ( farming methods focused on restoring soil health and enhancing biodiversity). 


 The campaign covers 34 States and Union Territories, over 700 districts and 50,000 villages. It aims to reach around 50 lakh farmers through coordinated activities. States and Union Territories have been instructed to prioritise 100 high fertiliser-consuming districts to strengthen outreach and promote balanced nutrient management.

The campaign deployed 1,657 multidisciplinary teams for direct field-level engagement. Additionally, 3,167 field demonstrations and 4,779 interactive programs provided hands-on learning. A further 4,916 Janpratinidhi Sammelans, including those involving fertiliser and input dealers, strengthened grassroots engagement.. Overall, the campaign directly reached around 1.07 crore farmers and other stakeholders, while social media outreach covered approximately 4.5 crore citizens.

 Western Coalfields Limited (WCL) a subsidiary of Coal India Limited under the Ministry of Coal, has emerged as a key growth driver of Coal India Limited (CIL), recording strong performance across coal production, offtake and overburden removal during the current financial year. From April to October 2026, WCL was the only subsidiary of CIL to exceed its targets in all three key operational parameters , achieving 102.47% of its production target, 108.82% of its offtake target and 104.56% of its overburden removal target. 


 The company's strong operational performance has significantly contributed to strengthening domestic coal availability and supporting India's energy security. WCL's additional production of 4.53 MT during April–October 2026 was higher than the entire net production growth of CIL during the corresponding period. 


 Strong Performance Across Key Parameters 


 WCL recorded particularly impressive growth during October 2026. Coal production increased to 5.93 MT , compared with 3.60 MT during the corresponding month last year, registering a growth of 64.87% , the highest among major CIL subsidiaries. The company also achieved 108.60% of its monthly production target. 


 Offtake during October increased to 6.67 MT , against 4.44 MT in the corresponding month last year, registering a growth of 50.16% . WCL was also the only major subsidiary to exceed its monthly offtake target, achieving 102.40%. 


 During the April–October period, WCL recorded: 


 
 32.96 MT coal production , registering a growth of 15.92% ; 

 41.56 MT offtake , registering a growth of 25.54% ; and 

 207.95 MCuM of overburden removal , registering a growth of 36.10% . 

 

 The company had also recorded the highest growth in both production and offtake among CIL subsidiaries during September 2026. 


 Record Stock Liquidation and Improved Coal Evacuation 


 A major achievement during the period has been WCL's substantial reduction in pithead coal stock. The stock was reduced from 13.034 MT on April 1, 2026 to 4.44 MT on October 31, 2026 , resulting in the liquidation of around 8.6 MT , or approximately 66% of the opening stock. 


 Enhanced coordination with the Railways and focused monitoring of rake placement and loading contributed significantly to this achievement. WCL loaded 6,146 rakes up to October 31, 2026, compared with 4,402 rakes during the corresponding period last year, registering an increase of 39.6% . 


 Rake loading to the power sector increased by 40.8% , while supplies to MAHAGENCO registered particularly strong growth. 


 Focused Monitoring and Mine-Level Decision Making 


 WCL's strong performance has been driven by intensive and continuous monitoring of operations at the mine level. Daily reviews of production, despatch and operational issues, regular meetings with Area General Managers, and frequent visits by senior management have enabled faster identification and resolution of operational bottlenecks. 


 The extension of monthly coordination and review mechanisms down to the mine level has strengthened accountability and ensured closer monitoring of critical activities across operations. 


 Close coordination with the Railways, State Governments and concerned Ministries has also facilitated the timely resolution of issues relating to environmental and forest clearances, land matters and other operational requirements. 


 During FY 2026–27, WCL has secured four environmental clearances or amendments and two forest clearances , helping ensure continuity of mining operations. 


 Technology, Quality and Operational Efficiency 


 WCL has continued to strengthen operational efficiency through improved transportation and loading infrastructure, including all-weather coal transportation roads, rapid loading systems and automated weighbridges. 


 The company currently has six Surface Miners and three Continuous Miners in operation . Focus on coal quality has also yielded positive results, with around 86% of sampled coal from April to October confirmed at its declared grade . 


 Focused operational improvements have also contributed to a significant reduction in overloading charges, while October despatches achieved 100% net realisation without debit loss . 


 Supporting Power Generation and Energy Security 


 The significant increase in WCL's offtake has directly supported power plants and industries. The additional coal supplies have strengthened domestic availability and contributed to reducing dependence on imported coal. 


 The additional rakes supplied to MAHAGENCO alone are estimated to have supported approximately 5,800 million units of additional power generation in Maharashtra . 


 WCL's Profit Before Tax for April–September 2026 stood at ₹1,352.26 crore , registering a growth of 76.3% over the corresponding period of the previous year. 


 Towards Aatmanirbhar and Viksit Bharat 


 WCL's performance during the current financial year demonstrates how focused leadership, intensive mine-level monitoring, faster decision-making and close coordination among stakeholders can translate into substantial operational outcomes. 


 With significant coal benches exposed in advance through record overburden removal, substantial reduction in pithead stocks, a motivated workforce and strong operational momentum, WCL is well positioned for sustained performance during the second half of the financial year. 


 WCL remains committed to powering the nation, strengthening India's energy security and contributing to the vision of an Aatmanirbhar and Viksit Bharat.

Posted On:
 02 NOV 2026 8:35PM by PIB Delhi
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi today inaugurated the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit & Expo 2026 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi. Addressing the gathering of industry leaders, investors, startup representatives, and senior officials from India and abroad, the Prime Minister noted that this year's summit takes place amid special circumstances dominated by global energy shocks that have underscored the vital importance of renewable energy in daily life and national development. He pointed out that the scope of this year's event is exceptionally broad as it coincides with the Ninth Assembly of the International Solar Alliance and includes delegates from the Fourth Conference on Green Hydrogen. 


 Stating that recent global disruptions have demonstrated the direct link between energy security and economic security, the Prime Minister warned that continued over-reliance on fossil fuels will repeatedly disrupt the world economy because fossil reserves are finite and concentrated in a few regions. He contrasted this vulnerability with the boundless, universally accessible potential of clean energy. “And we all know, the future of Energy Security lies in Clean Energy,” asserted Shri Modi. 


 Stating that the new era of the solar revolution relies on innovation as much as adoption, the Prime Minister urged startups, IITs, innovators, and entrepreneurs to design round-the-clock, all-weather solar models capable of meeting maximum household needs, including rooftop solar cooking to minimize reliance on imported gas and home solar charging for electric two-wheelers and cars. “Through this, middle-class families of the country can save thousands of rupees every year,” noted Shri Modi. 


 Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy, Education and Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, Shri Pralhad Joshi, highlighted India's remarkable progress in the renewable energy sector and the transformative role of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi's leadership in shaping the country's energy landscape, while addressing the event. 


 At the outset, the Union Minister expressed his appreciation for the visionary leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, stating that he had given India's energy sector a new energy, direction and confidence. 


 He further highlighted that Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi approved the Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana with an outlay of more than ₹5,000 crore, under which 5,000 MW of floating solar capacity will be developed. He also noted that the Prime Minister had recently approved the Green Energy Corridor Phase-III, with an investment of ₹1.86 lakh crore. 


 The Union Minister stated that the ideas tested and proven in Gujarat were scaled up at the national level after Shri Narendra Modi became Prime Minister, giving India's renewable energy journey a new direction and momentum. 


 Highlighting India's economic growth and rising energy requirements, Shri Joshi said that India is today one of the world's fastest-growing major economies. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has revised India's growth forecast for 2026-27 to 7 per cent. He emphasised that this economic growth is also accompanied by increasing energy demand, which necessitates renewable energy to meet the country's requirements sustainably. 


 Shri Pralhad Joshi stated that in September 2024 India's non-fossil fuel-based installed capacity had crossed 200 GW. He highlighted that the capacity had since reached 310 GW, representing an addition of more than 110 GW in two years. He further stated that, under the guidance of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, PM Surya Ghar had crossed 65 lakh installations, with more than one lakh installations taking place every six days. 


 Highlighting the investment in the RE sector, Shri Joshi said that the total investment has crossed USD 67 billion within the last two years, making it the biggest investment in any sector. He also noted that the sector had attracted USD 6.2 billion in Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) over the last two years. He stated that this reflected the growing confidence of investors in the sector. 


 Underscoring India's progress in the renewable energy sector over the last 12 years, the Minister stated that the country's non-fossil fuel-based installed capacity had increased from 80.3 GW to more than 310 GW, registering a growth of 280 per cent. Solar capacity had risen from 2.8 GW to 171 GW, marking an increase of 5,800 per cent, while wind capacity had grown from 21 GW to 60 GW, registering a growth of 176 per cent. 


 He further highlighted that India's solar module manufacturing capacity had increased from 2 GW to 225 GW, registering a growth of 11,150 per cent, while solar cell manufacturing capacity had risen from zero to 45 GW. Wind turbine manufacturing capacity has also increased from 10 GW to 24 GW. 


 Highlighting the reduction in renewable energy costs, Shri Joshi stated that solar tariffs had declined from ₹10-11 per unit in 2011-12 to ₹2.15 per unit in 2024-25. He further noted that green hydrogen was available at ₹279/kg, the lowest price globally, while green ammonia had reached ₹49.75/kg, also the lowest price globally. Highlighting India's leadership in the global green hydrogen sector, Shri Joshi stated that India is number one in the world in green hydrogen offtake commitments. 


 Emphasising the scale and pace of India's achievements, the Union Minister said, "This is Scale. This is Speed. This is Aatma Nirbharta. And this is the energy of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi." 


 Shri Joshi stated that BRE Summit and Expo 2026 is an important platform for strengthening this investment ecosystem. He invited investors from across the world to participate in India's renewable energy journey, saying, "Invest in India. Innovate in India. Grow with India."

 Ministry of Tribal Affairs in collaboration with the ICMR–National Institute of Health Research (ICMR-NIHR), Bhubaneswar under the Janjatiya Health Institutional Transformation (JanHIT) initiative, has organised the 1 st of its kind National Orientation Programme for Tribal Healers on Public Health on 1–2 nd November 2026 at Kanha Shanti Vanam, Hyderabad. The programme was inaugurated at the auditorium of Kanha Shanti Vanam, Hyderabad by Shri. Manish Thakur, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs and Dr. Sanghamitra Pati, Director, ICMR-NIHR, Bhubaneswar in presence of Shri B. M. Santosh, IAS, Special Secretary and Director, Tribal Welfare, Telangana, Dr. V. Samujwala, Director, Tribal Cultural Research & Training Institute (TCR&TI), Telangana, and other senior officials from Ministry of Tribal Affairs and ICMR-NIHR, Bhubaneswar. The launch of this landmark initiative on the first day of the Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas Pakhwada underscores the shared commitment to honouring and empowering India's tribal communities through inclusive health and capacity-building interventions. 


 


 The 1 st phase of the orientation programme is being attended by around 550 tribal healers nominated by the State Tribal Welfare departments from nine states and UTs of India (Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Karnataka, Keralam, Maharashtra, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli). The orientation programme aims to orient tribal healers on key public health issues and strengthen their understanding of common diseases, early identification of danger signs, and appropriate referral for timely medical care. Recognising the important role of healers in tribal communities, the initiative seeks to enhance their awareness of essential health practices and encourage linkages with the formal healthcare system. 


 The two-day orientation programme will cover three training modules addressing a wide range of public health concerns. These include communicable and vector-borne diseases, skin diseases, non-communicable diseases, metabolic and blood disorders, liver diseases, and mental health conditions. The sessions will also focus on appropriate referral for snakebites, scorpion & other stings, animal bites, injuries, eye and ear disorders; oral health; and newborn and infant care. The training will also include integrated practice, review sessions, a post-training assessment, and participant feedback to reinforce learning and assess the orientation's effectiveness. 


 Participants from different states will attend the 2 day programme, with state-wise arrangements for training sessions in regional languages to facilitate effective communication and learning. Experts from AIIMS, ICMR, Quality Control of India, MS Swaminathan Foundation, Amrita Institute, Kochi, IIHMR, Bengaluru and Piramal Swasthya, Maharashtra will be delivering sessions in respective languages for the healers. 


 By orienting tribal healers on essential health concerns and appropriate referral practices, the programme seeks to promote informed community-level health support and strengthen collaboration between tribal community practices and the formal healthcare system. This structured capacity-building module developed by ICMR-NIHR, Bhubaneswar, with support from MoTA represents a milestone effort to integrate tribal healthcare practices with formal medical systems, particularly as we commemorate Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas. 


 The programme will conclude on 2 nd November 2026 with a closing ceremony and distribution of certificates to participants.

 The conference commenced with a welcome address by Ms. Shoko Ishikawa , Country Representative, UN Women India, who emphasised the importance of gender-disaggregated data and bridging the gap between data producers and users. Mr. Jean-Eric Paque , Ambassador of the European Union (EU) to India, highlighted the EU–India Strategic Partnership in advancing gender equality and women’s economic participation. Dr. Preetam B. Yashvant , Joint Secretary, Ministry of Women and Child Development, also addressed the gathering, followed by Dr. Dalip Singh, Director General (Central Statistics), MoSPI , who emphasised identifying gender gaps to inform evidence-based policies. Dr. Shamika Ravi , Member, Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister, highlighted progress in welfare delivery and women’s financial empowerment, while stressing the need for improved employment quality, state-level analysis and stronger gender statistics to guide policy reforms. The inaugural session concluded with a vote of thanks by Ms. Supriya Roy, Additional Director General, MoSPI , who acknowledged the contributions of speakers, participants and UN Women. 


 The conference featured four thematic technical sessions , focusing on health and survival across the life course; girls’ education, learning and transition; women’s work, wages, formality and care; and women’s livelihoods, enterprises, skills and financial inclusion. The sessions brought together experts, policymakers and practitioners to examine key findings from Women and Men in India 2025 , identify differences in outcomes between women and men, and explore opportunities for translating statistical evidence into actionable policy insights. 


 Discussions on health and survival recognised progress in maternal healthcare and essential health services, while highlighting nutritional and adolescent health challenges. The session on girls’ education, learning and transition noted improvements in enrolment, while emphasising gaps in learning outcomes, STEM participation and employment pathways. 


 Deliberations on women’s work, wages, formality and care acknowledged rising female labour-force participation, while highlighting challenges in job quality, wage disparities and unpaid care work. The session on women’s livelihoods, enterprises, skills and financial inclusion recognised progress in entrepreneurship and financial inclusion, while stressing the need for better access to credit, markets and sustainable livelihoods, alongside women’s agency and safety. 


 During the valedictory session, Ms. Suhela Khan, Country Programme Manager, Women’s Economic Empowerment, UN Women India, and Ms. Geeta Singh Rathore, Director General (NSS), MoSPI, highlighted the need to address persistent gender disparities in health, education and economic participation, with particular emphasis on quality of employment, unpaid care work and financial inclusion. The discussions also provided valuable inputs for future editions of Women and Men in India , particularly the 2026 edition, underscoring the importance of improved measurement of gender gaps, strengthened inter-ministerial coordination and evidence-based policymaking. The conference concluded with a vote of thanks delivered by Ms. Sunitha Bhaskar, Additional Director General, MoSPI. 


 


 The conference concluded by reaffirming the importance of strengthening India's gender statistical ecosystem and fostering continued collaboration among government institutions, statistical agencies, researchers and development partners. It underscored the need to translate gender-disaggregated data into meaningful policy insights to support inclusive development and advancing gender equality.

items.title: TRAI issues the Telecom Consumers Complaint Redressal (Fourth Amendment) Regulations, 2026
key_lines: The existing alternative criterion based on annual financial turnover exceeding ₹5 crore has been dispensed with thus simplifying the applicability clause.
items.text:
Posted On:
 02 NOV 2026 6:08PM by PIB Delhi
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has today issued the Telecom Consumers Complaint Redressal (Fourth Amendment) Regulations, 2026. 


 To address the evolving needs related to the upgradation of grievance redressal framework, the Authority released a consultation paper on the Draft Telecom Consumers Complaint Redressal (Fourth Amendment) Regulations, 2026, on 7 th May 2026, inviting comments and counter-comments by 12 th and 19 th June 2026, respectively. A total of 32 comments and 24 counter-comments were received from stakeholders and uploaded to the TRAI website. An online Open House Discussion (OHD) was held on 17 th July 2026. 


 Based on the above consultations, the Authority has finalized the Amendment Regulations. The salient features of the same are given below: 


 
 The amended regulations shall apply to Internet Service Providers having more than ten thousand subscribers as on the last day of the preceding financial year. The existing alternative criterion based on annual financial turnover exceeding ₹5 crore has been dispensed with thus simplifying the applicability clause. 

 Consumers will now be able to register complaints and appeals, raise service requests, and make service-related queries through the service provider’s mobile application, in addition to the existing channels of the Complaint Centre, website and web portal thus giving wider choice, flexibility and ease to consumers in filing complaint and appeal. 

 Consumer support through Complaint Centres will be available round the clock on all days of the week, instead of the existing 16-hour arrangement. Such support may be provided through human representatives, automated systems, AI agents, other customer-centric technological solutions, or a combination thereof. Human assistance shall be available for at least sixteen hours daily. Technology-based solutions shall function with appropriate human oversight. This will ensure ease and convenience to consumers and gives flexibility to service providers in manning the Complaint Centres. 

 Every service provider shall equip dedicated desks or helplines in their Complaint Centre or Consumer support centres, with personnel or assistive technology capable of receiving calls from persons with disabilities (PwDs). Service providers will ensure that their mobile app, website and portal have accessibility features in accordance with the applicable guidelines or standards on accessibility for Persons with Disabilities issued by the Government of India. 

 The time limit for filing an appeal following disposal of a complaint has been revised from 30 days to 15 days as consumers would normally prefer appeal as soon as possible whereas a longer time allowed unduly increases compliance requirements. Consumers may now file appeals through the service provider’s mobile application, website or portal, in addition to the existing channels of email, post, in person, or through the Consumer Care Number. This will ensure faster resolution of appeal. 

 Also, the Appellate Authority has been made more responsible through the present amendment. It has been mandated that the Appellate Authority shall comprise one or more persons who are regular employees in the management of the service provider and also possess at least five years’ experience. The Appellate Authority shall examine the appeal, take appropriate action for resolution of the grievance, and communicate its final decision within 15 days of receipt of the appeal. 

 The earlier process of resolution of appeal cases through Advisory committee has been dispensed with in order to ensure efficient and time-bound resolution of appeal cases. 

 A new mechanism of “Feedback Survey” has been introduced. Upon resolution or closure of a complaint or appeal, the service provider shall conduct an online feedback survey to assess the consumer’s satisfaction with the resolution. Feedback shall be obtained on a five-point scale, ranging from “Fully Satisfied” (5 points) to “Totally Dissatisfied” (1 point). The service provider shall publish the results of such feedback surveys on its website on a quarterly basis. 

 It has also been mandated that every service provider shall place before its CEO or Board of Directors a quarterly report on the redressal of complaints, appeals and the results of feedback survey. This has been done to ensure suitable review and oversight of the disposal of complaints and appeals by the service providers at the highest level. 

 A new mechanism of Consumer Grievance Redressal Oversight Committee has been introduced. Every Service Provider shall establish a Consumer Grievance Redressal Oversight Committee to oversee and periodically review the functioning of its grievance redressal mechanism. The Committee shall comprise representatives of the Service Provider and at least one representative from each consumer organisation registered with the Authority in the State or Union Territory forming part of the licensed service area. Service Providers will form such committee taking representation mandatorily from those states and union territories in which their subscriber base is above ten thousand. The Committee shall meet at least once every year to review the grievance redressal mechanism. 

 The amendment introduces a new mechanism of Regulatory Review. The Authority may conduct periodic review of the functioning of the Grievance Redressal Mechanism of the service providers by: - 
 
 audit and inspection of the records of the service provider, 

 audit and analysis of Quarterly Performance Reports submitted by the service provider, 

 review based on consumer feedback. 

 
 

 The amendment introduces the provision of financial disincentives in cases of disposal of complaint or appeal in contravention of the provisions of these regulations observed during the audit, inspection, analysis or review.
